title: Developmental Botany

toc.title: 14.4 Monocot and dicot embryos; types and functions of endosperm

html:
Developmental Botany carries 2 of the 40 Botany questions and is the story of how a flower makes a seed: the asexual shortcuts plants take, the manufacture of the two gametophytes by sporogenesis and gametogenesis, pollination and double fertilization, and what the products become — dicot and monocot embryos and the endosperm.

The questions are unfailingly about ploidy (which cells are n, 2n, 3n), about names (tapetum, scutellum, geitonogamy, chalazogamy) and about the arithmetic of meiosis — how many mother cells a given number of seeds requires.

What the paper asks from this chapter
  • Asexual reproduction — rhizome (ginger), tuber (potato eyes), bulb (onion), corm (Colocasia), runner, sucker, offset, leaf buds (Bryophyllum); cutting, layering, grafting; apomixis and nucellar polyembryony (citrus).
  • Male side — anther wall (epidermis, endothecium, middle layers, tapetum = nutritive); PMC 2n → meiosis → tetrad of 4 microspores (n); exine of sporopollenin over intine; vegetative (tube) cell + generative cell → 2 male gametes; shed at 2- or 3-celled stage.
  • Female side — ovule (funicle, integuments, micropyle, chalaza, nucellus); commonest anatropous; MMC 2n → meiosis → 4 megaspores, one functional → 3 mitoses → Polygonum-type, 7-celled, 8-nucleate embryo sac (egg + 2 synergids with filiform apparatus; central cell with 2 polar nuclei; 3 antipodals).
  • Pollination — autogamy, geitonogamy (agent needed but genetically self), xenogamy; anemophily, hydrophily, entomophily, ornithophily, chiropterophily; contrivances: dicliny, dichogamy (protandry Salvia, protogyny Plantago), herkogamy, heterostyly, self-incompatibility; cleistogamy.
  • Double fertilization (Nawaschin, 1898) — syngamy (n + n = 2n zygote) + triple fusion (n + n + n = 3n endosperm nucleus); entry by porogamy, chalazogamy (Casuarina), mesogamy (Cucurbita).
  • Embryos — dicot (Capsella): basal cell → suspensor, apical → globular → heart → two cotyledons, plumule terminal; monocot: one cotyledon = scutellum, plumule in coleoptile, radicle in coleorhiza, epiblast.
  • Endosperm (3n) — nuclear (coconut water), cellular (Datura), helobial; albuminous vs exalbuminous seeds; aleurone layer; perisperm (2n) from nucellus (black pepper).

14.1 Asexual reproduction

In vegetative propagation an ordinary organ — root, stem, leaf or bud — grows into a whole plant identical to the parent:

Organ Structure Example
Underground stem rhizome ginger, turmeric
tuber potato (the "eyes" are buds)
bulb onion, garlic
corm Colocasia, Crocus
Sub-aerial stem runner Cynodon (dubo grass)
sucker mint, chrysanthemum
offset water hyacinth Eichhornia
Leaf adventitious marginal buds Bryophyllum pinnatum
Root adventitious buds sweet potato, Dahlia

Growers copy the trick artificially: cutting (sugarcane, rose), layering (jasmine, litchi), grafting and budding (mango, citrus, apple in Mustang and Jumla) and micropropagation by tissue culture (Unit 15).

Apomixis is asexual reproduction wearing the disguise of seed: an embryo forms without fertilization, so the seedling clones its mother.

In nucellar polyembryony (citrus, mango) extra embryos sprout from the nucellus beside the sexual embryo. Breeders covet apomixis because it could fix hybrid vigour permanently — the hybrid would breed true from its own seed.

The trade-off is standard exam fare: asexual offspring are quick and exactly like the prized parent (and the only route for seedless kinds such as banana), but with no variation one new disease can take the whole plantation; sexual reproduction is slower and needs pollinators, but variation is the raw material of breeding and evolution.

Ploidy arithmetic of the sac

Problem. A species' endosperm holds 24 chromosomes. State the chromosome numbers of(a) the embryo,(b) an antipodal cell,(c) the megaspore mother cell. Separately: how many meiotic divisions were needed to make 100 seeds' worth of female and male gametophytes? Solution. Endosperm is 3n = 24, so n = 8: (a) embryo 2n = 16; (b) antipodals are haploid, 8; (c) the megaspore mother cell is 2n = 16. For 100 seeds: each embryo sac costs one megaspore meiosis (three products wasted) → 100; each anther meiosis yields four pollen grains → 100 ÷ 4 = 25; total 125 meiotic divisions — the classic asymmetry the paper tests.

14.2 Sporogenesis and gametogenesis in angiosperms

The plant in the field is the diploid sporophyte; the pollen grain and the embryo sac are the reduced haploid gametophytes, kept inside it. Angiosperms are heterosporous: the anther (microsporangium) makes microspores, the ovule (megasporangium) makes megaspores.

The male side — anther to pollen

An anther typically has two lobes, each with two pollen sacs.

Its wall has four layers: epidermis, endothecium (whose fibrous thickenings spring the sac open at dehiscence), middle layers, and innermost the tapetum — dense, often multinucleate cells that nourish the developing spores and supply sporopollenin and wall proteins.

If the tapetum fails, the pollen is sterile; protection is the outer layers' business, not the tapetum's.

Inside, each pollen (microspore) mother cell (2n) undergoes meiosis — microsporogenesis — to give a tetrad of four haploid microspores.

Each matures into a pollen grain walled by the sculptured outer exine of near-indestructible sporopollenin (pollen survives in sediments for millennia, the basis of palynology) over a pectin– cellulose intine.

Microgametogenesis: the microspore nucleus divides unequally into a large vegetative (tube) cell and a small generative cell; the generative cell later divides into the two male gametes.

In about 60% of families pollen is shed at the 2-celled stage. The mature male gametophyte is thus only three cells.

The female side — ovule to embryo sac

The ovule hangs in the ovary on its stalk, the funicle; its body of parenchyma, the nucellus, is wrapped in one or two integuments leaving a pore, the micropyle, at the tip; the base opposite the micropyle is the chalaza.

In the commonest form, the anatropous ovule, the body is inverted so the micropyle faces the funicle (others: orthotropous in Polygonum, campylotropous in pea family).

An archesporial cell in the nucellus becomes the megaspore mother cell (2n), whose meiosis — megasporogenesis — gives a linear tetrad of four megaspores.

Typically three (the micropylar ones) degenerate and one functional (chalazal) megaspore remains.

Its nucleus divides by three successive mitoses — megagametogenesis — to eight nuclei, which wall off into the Polygonum-type embryo sac: 7 cells, 8 nuclei:

  • At the micropylar end, the egg apparatus: the egg cell flanked by two synergids bearing the filiform apparatus that guides the pollen tube.
  • In the middle, the large central cell with two polar nuclei (which may fuse into a diploid secondary nucleus before fertilization).
  • At the chalazal end, three antipodal cells.

The ploidy map

Everything belonging to the sporophyte — nucellus, integuments, both mother cells, later the seed coat and fruit wall — is 2n.

Everything inside the pollen grain and embryo sac is n (the central cell carries two n nuclei, becoming 2n only if they fuse as the secondary nucleus). The zygote and embryo are 2n again; the endosperm is 3n.

A perisperm (next section) is 2n — it is nucellus, not endosperm.

14.3 Pollination and fertilization

Pollination is the transfer of pollen from anther to stigma — the obligatory first step, since the non-motile male gametes can travel only inside a pollen tube.

Within one flower it is autogamy (self-pollination); between flowers of the same plant geitonogamy (an agent is needed, but genetically it is still selfing); to another plant of the species, xenogamy (cross-pollination), the only kind bringing new genes.

Selfing is guaranteed by homogamy (sexes mature together), bud pollination (pea, wheat) and cleistogamy — flowers that never open (Commelina, Viola, Oxalis), which set seed even without a single pollinator.

Cross-pollination needs an agent, and flowers advertise accordingly:

Agent Name Syndrome Examples
Wind anemophily dull, nectarless; torrents of light dry pollen; feathery stigma maize, grasses, Pinus
Water hydrophily unwettable, often thread-like pollen Vallisneria, Hydrilla, Zostera
Insects entomophily coloured, scented, nectar; sticky spiny pollen mustard, Salvia, fig and its wasp
Birds ornithophily big red tubes, watery nectar, no scent Bombax (simal), Butea
Bats chiropterophily large, dull, musky, opening at night Kigelia, Adansonia

Plants also evolve contrivances against selfing: dicliny (unisexual flowers — monoecious maize, dioecious papaya), dichogamy (protandry, anthers first: sunflower, Salvia; protogyny, stigma first: Plantago, Michelia), herkogamy (physical barriers, Calotropis), heterostyly (pin and thrum styles, Primula) and self-incompatibility, a genetic block on own-pollen tubes (tobacco, crucifers).

Continuous selfing gives purity but inbreeding depression; crossing gives variation and hybrid vigour at the price of wasted pollen and dependence on agents.

Fertilization. On a receptive stigma the pollen hydrates and the intine grows out as the pollen tube, tube nucleus at the tip, the two male gametes behind, digesting through the style towards synergid signals.

It enters the ovule usually by the micropyle (porogamy), sometimes through the chalaza (chalazogamy, Casuarina) or through integument/funicle (mesogamy, Cucurbita), discharges into one synergid, and the angiosperm signature follows (discovered by Nawaschin, 1898, in Lilium and Fritillaria):

Double fertilization

Syngamy — one male gamete (n) + egg (n) → zygote (2n) → embryo. Triple fusion — the second male gamete (n) + two polar nuclei (n + n) → primary endosperm nucleus (3n) → endosperm.

The economy is the point: the nutritive endosperm is manufactured only when an embryo has actually been formed — no fertilisation, no wasted food (contrast the gymnosperms' endosperm-equivalent, the female gametophyte, made in advance regardless).

Worked example — the meiosis bill for a hundred seeds

Problem. A fruit contains 100 seeds. Assuming every pollen grain and ovule was used, find(a) the minimum number of pollen grains needed,(b) the number of meiotic divisions in the anthers,(c) the number of meiotic divisions in the ovules, and(d) the total.

Solution. Each seed needs one embryo sac (one egg) and one pollen tube carrying two male gametes.

(a) One pollen grain per ovule: 100 pollen grains.

(b) Each pollen mother cell's meiosis gives four microspores, so 100 / 4 = 25 meiotic divisions in the anthers.

(c) Each megaspore mother cell's meiosis gives only one functional megaspore (three degenerate), so 100 ovules cost 100 meiotic divisions.

(d) Total 25 + 100 = 125 meiotic divisions — the female side is four times as expensive per seed as the male.

14.4 Monocot and dicot embryos; types and functions of endosperm

The zygote divides transversely into a basal cell (towards the micropyle) and an apical cell.

In the model dicot Capsella bursa-pastoris the basal cell builds a filamentous suspensor that thrusts the embryo into the nutritive endosperm (and often absorbs food itself), while the apical cell builds the embryo proper: globular stage → heart-shaped stage as the two cotyledons bulge out → mature embryo with two lateral cotyledons, a terminal plumule between them, hypocotyl and radicle.

The monocot embryo bears a single terminal-looking cotyledon, the shield-shaped scutellum, pressed against the endosperm to absorb its contents; the plumule sits laterally inside its hollow sheath, the coleoptile (the spear that pierces the soil at germination), and the radicle is capped by the coleorhiza; a small flap opposite the scutellum, the epiblast, is often read as the vestige of the second cotyledon.

Feature Dicot embryo Monocot embryo
Cotyledons two, lateral one — the scutellum
Plumule terminal, exposed lateral, inside coleoptile
Radicle exposed inside coleorhiza
Epiblast absent present (grasses)

The primary endosperm nucleus (3n) meanwhile divides to feed the embryo, in one of three patterns:

  • Nuclear endosperm — free nuclear divisions first (a multinucleate soup), walls formed later from the outside in, or never: the commonest type (cereals, Capsella). Coconut "water" is free-nuclear endosperm; the white kernel is its later cellular part.
  • Cellular endosperm — a wall after every division from the start (Datura, Petunia).
  • Helobial endosperm — intermediate: the first division walls off two unequal chambers, the larger then going free-nuclear (order Helobiales).

Seeds that keep the endosperm at maturity are endospermic (albuminous) — cereals (whose outermost endosperm layer is the protein-rich aleurone met in Unit 13), castor, coconut.

In non-endospermic (exalbuminous) seeds — pea, bean, gram — the endosperm is consumed during development and the cotyledons become the store.

Where the nucellus itself persists and stores food, it is a perisperm (black pepper, beet, cardamom) — diploid maternal tissue, not endosperm at all.

The endosperm's functions: nourish the embryo in the seed and (in albuminous seeds) through germination, regulate embryo growth hormonally, and stand as the triploid arena in which so much of our food — wheat flour, rice, maize — actually resides.

Common mistake

Four pairs the paper swaps: geitonogamy looks like cross-pollination but is genetically self (same plant's genotype); the coconut's liquid is nuclear endosperm, not cell sap; coleoptile sheathes the plumule, coleorhiza the radicle — both monocot-only; and endosperm is 3n while the embryo beside it is 2n, because triple fusion and syngamy used different partners in the same sac.

Endosperm ploidy when parent ploidies differ

Problem. A tetraploid female plant (4n = 48) is pollinated by a diploid male plant (2n = 24). Find the chromosome number of the zygote and the primary endosperm nucleus (PEN).

Solution. The tetraploid female produces a diploid egg (2n = 24) and two diploid polar nuclei (2n + 2n = 4n = 48). The diploid male produces haploid male gametes (n = 12).

Thus the zygote has 2n + n = 24 + 12 = \mathbf{36} chromosomes (3n), while the PEN has 4n + n = 48 + 12 = \mathbf{60} chromosomes (5n).

Formula and fact sheet

  • Asexual gallery: rhizome ginger; tuber potato; bulb onion; corm Colocasia; runner Cynodon; sucker mint; offset Eichhornia; leaf buds Bryophyllum; apomixis = seed without fertilization (citrus nucellar embryos).
  • Male: tapetum feeds, endothecium opens; 1 PMC (2n) → meiosis → 4 microspores; exine sporopollenin; tube cell + generative cell → 2 gametes.
  • Female: 1 MMC (2n) → meiosis → 4 megaspores, 1 functional → 3 mitoses → 7 cells / 8 nuclei (Polygonum type); anatropous ovule commonest.
  • Pollination words: autogamy/geitonogamy/xenogamy; agents anemo-, hydro-, entomo-, ornitho-, chiropterophily; protandry sunflower, protogyny Plantago; cleistogamy Viola.
  • Double fertilization (Nawaschin 1898): syngamy n+n=2n embryo; triple fusion n+n+n=3n endosperm; entry porogamy (usual), chalazogamy Casuarina, mesogamy Cucurbita.
  • Embryos: dicot — suspensor + 2 cotyledons + terminal plumule (Capsella); monocot — scutellum, coleoptile, coleorhiza, epiblast.
  • Endosperm 3n: nuclear (coconut water), cellular (Datura), helobial; albuminous (cereals, castor) vs exalbuminous (pea, bean); perisperm 2n = nucellus (black pepper).
  • Arithmetic: 1 seed = 1 ovule + 1 pollen grain; pollen meioses = seeds/4; ovule meioses = seeds; ploidy: sporophyte parts 2n, gametophyte parts n, embryo 2n, endosperm 3n.

Rapid-revision tables and high-yield facts

Item Value
Pollen wall exine sporopollenin; intine cellulose
Microspore mother cell → pollen meiosis, 4 per meiosis
Megaspores 4 made, 1 functional
Embryo sac 7 cells, 8 nuclei
Egg apparatus egg + 2 synergids (filiform apparatus)
Double fertilisation syngamy 2n + triple fusion 3n (Nawaschin)

Albuminous / exalbuminous castor, maize, wheat / pea, bean, mango
Monocot sheaths coleoptile (plumule), coleorhiza (radicle)

Chapter summary

  • Plants clone themselves by rhizomes, tubers, bulbs, runners, leaf buds and even apomictic seed — fast and faithful, but variation-free; growers exploit the same tricks by cutting, layering and grafting.
  • The anther's tapetum feeds microspores produced four-at-a-time by PMC meiosis; each becomes a sporopollenin-armoured pollen grain carrying a tube cell and a generative cell (source of the two gametes).
  • The ovule's single functional megaspore builds, by three mitoses, the 7-celled, 8-nucleate Polygonum embryo sac — egg apparatus, central cell with two polar nuclei, three antipodals.
  • Pollination spans autogamy to xenogamy on wind, water, insects, birds and bats, with cleistogamy guaranteeing selfing and dicliny, dichogamy, herkogamy, heterostyly and self-incompatibility enforcing crossing.
  • Double fertilization — syngamy making the 2n zygote, triple fusion the 3n endosperm — is unique to angiosperms and economical: food tissue is made only when an embryo exists.
  • The dicot embryo (suspensor, two cotyledons, terminal plumule) contrasts with the monocot's scutellum, coleoptile and coleorhiza.
  • Endosperm develops by nuclear, cellular or helobial patterns and may persist (albuminous seeds, with aleurone in cereals) or be absorbed into the cotyledons (exalbuminous); perisperm is persistent 2n nucellus, not endosperm.

Answers and explanations — Set A

1. (b) — Each eye is a bud in the axil of a scale leaf on the stem tuber.

2. (d) — Plantlets sprout from notches on the Bryophyllum leaf margin and drop off ready-rooted.

3. (c) — An apomictic embryo (e.g. from the nucellus) clones the mother although it arrives inside a seed.

4. (c) — The tapetum feeds the spores and donates sporopollenin; protection belongs to the outer wall layers.

5. (a) — Sporopollenin resists decay for millennia, preserving pollen in sediments.

6. (b) — Meiosis of one diploid PMC yields a tetrad of four haploid microspores.

7. (d) — The generative cell divides mitotically into the two male gametes; the tube cell makes the tube.

8. (c) — Inverted ovules (micropyle facing the funicle) occur in most angiosperms.

9. (b) — One nucleus → 2 → 4 → 8 nuclei, which then organise into seven cells.

10. (a) — Egg + 2 synergids + central cell (2 nuclei) + 3 antipodals: 7 cells, 8 nuclei.

11. (d) — Finger-like wall ingrowths at the synergid tips secrete the tube's guidance chemicals.

12. (b) — It requires a pollinating agent but is genetically self-pollination — a favourite distinction.

13. (c) — Maize pours light dry pollen from versatile anthers onto feathery silks.

14. (c) — Sunflower florets shed pollen before their stigmas become receptive; Plantago is the protogynous opposite.

15. (a) — S. G. Nawaschin, 1898, working on Lilium and Fritillaria.

16. (b) — Gamete (n) + two polar nuclei (n + n) make the triploid endosperm mother nucleus.

17. (d) — Chalazogamy in Casuarina; mesogamy is Cucurbita's route, porogamy almost everybody else's.

18. (a) — The shield-like scutellum absorbs endosperm for the embryo; coleoptile and coleorhiza are sheaths.

19. (c) — The syncytial liquid endosperm before walls form the solid white kernel.

20. (a) — Persistent nucellus (2n maternal tissue), distinct from the 3n endosperm.

Answers and explanations — Set B

1. (c) — Pollinator or not, the genes come from one genotype; only xenogamy imports new ones.

2. (a) — Closed flowers self-pollinate in the bud: assured seed at the cost of variation.

3. (a) — Starved microspores abort — one basis of cytoplasmic and genic male sterility used in hybrid seed production.

4. (d) — A molecular identity check stops self tubes in the style, forcing outcrossing.

5. (c) — Triple fusion happens in the same event as syngamy, so provisioning tracks success exactly.

6. (c) — Three haploid genomes meet: two maternal (polar) and one paternal (gamete).

7. (b) — It is a living umbilical ram and, in many plants, an absorbing haustorium as well.

8. (d) — The embryo eats the endosperm as it grows and banks the reserves in its own cotyledons.

9. (d) — Clonal seed would let farmers replant hybrid seed without it segregating.

10. (a) — Anemophily is artillery, not marksmanship: numbers substitute for aim.

11. (b) — Two separate n nuclei (sometimes pre-fused into a 2n secondary nucleus) — not yet the 3n product.

12. (b) — The tough hollow cone takes the abrasion while the plumule rides inside.

Answers and explanations — Set C

1. (d) — One pollen tube per ovule delivers the two gametes a single seed needs.

2. (a) — Each PMC meiosis makes four grains: 400 / 4 = 100.

3. (b) — Endosperm is 3n: 3 \times 12 = 36 chromosomes.

4. (a) — The aleurone is the outermost endosperm layer, hence triploid like the rest of it.

5. (c) — Egg + two polar nuclei from the sac, plus the two male gametes: five nuclei in two fusions.

6. (b) — 40 pollen grains suffice, at four grains per PMC meiosis: 40 / 4 = 10.

7. (d) — The micropylar trio: egg flanked by two synergids with their filiform apparatus.

8. (c) — Antipodals are gametophyte cells, haploid: 18 / 2 = 9 chromosomes.

Group D — Model answers for long questions (10 marks each, for deeper revision)

  1. Describe the development of the male and female gametophytes in an angiosperm. [10]
  2. Describe pollination, double fertilisation and the development of the seed and fruit, and note apomixis and polyembryony. [10]

Model answer D1: microsporogenesis and megasporogenesis (10 marks)

Introduction. The flower is the reproductive organ of angiosperms, with sepals (calyx), petals (corolla), stamens (androecium) and carpels (gynoecium). The sporophyte makes spores by meiosis, and the spores grow into the gametophytes.

Male gametophyte (microsporogenesis).

  1. A young anther is tetrasporangiate (four pollen sacs, bilobed). The wall has the epidermis, endothecium, middle layers and the nutritive tapetum.
  2. The central sporogenous tissue forms microspore mother cells (pollen mother cells, 2n), each of which divides by meiosis into a tetrad of four haploid microspores.
  3. Each microspore becomes a pollen grain with a double wall: the tough exine (of sporopollenin) and the thin intine. The nucleus divides by mitosis to give a large vegetative cell and a small generative cell. The generative cell later divides into two male gametes.
  4. A pollen grain is the male gametophyte, and it is shed at the 2-celled or 3-celled stage.

Female gametophyte (megasporogenesis).

  1. The ovule has a stalk (funicle), integuments, a micropyle and the nucellus. A megaspore mother cell (2n) forms in the nucellus.
  2. Meiosis gives four megaspores, of which three degenerate and one at the chalazal end functions.
  3. The functional megaspore divides by three mitotic divisions to give 8 nuclei in the embryo sac (the female gametophyte, monosporic, Polygonum type).
  4. The final arrangement is 7 cells and 8 nuclei:
Position Cells
Micropylar end egg apparatus: one egg and two synergids
Centre central cell with two polar nuclei
Chalazal end three antipodal cells

Contrast.

Feature Male gametophyte Female gametophyte
Spore microspore megaspore
Number of spores that work all 4 1 of 4
Mature structure 2 or 3 celled pollen grain 7 cells, 8 nuclei
Location anther ovule in ovary

Numerical. 100 pollen mother cells make 400 pollen grains. A plant with 2n = 24 has n = 12 in the pollen. A flower with 4 stamens, each with 4 pollen sacs holding 1000 grains, produces 16\,000 pollen grains.

A single megaspore mother cell gives 1 embryo sac of 8 nuclei.

Conclusion. Meiosis makes four spores in both cases, but only the pollen gets all four to work, while in the ovule only one forms the embryo sac.

Model answer D2: pollination, double fertilisation and seed and fruit (10 marks)

Introduction. Pollination is the transfer of pollen from the anther to the stigma. Self-pollination (autogamy) occurs in the same flower and cross-pollination (allogamy) between flowers of different plants.

Agents.

Agent Name Flower features Example
Wind anemophily small, no scent, feathery stigma, light pollen maize, grasses
Insect entomophily colour, scent, nectar, sticky pollen rose, mustard
Water hydrophily pollen without wall Vallisneria
Bird ornithophily red, tubular bottlebrush
Bat chiropterophily night-opening banana, Kigelia

Devices for cross-pollination: dichogamy, self-incompatibility, herkogamy and unisexual flowers (dioecy as in papaya). Cleistogamous flowers never open.

Double fertilisation (Nawaschin, 1898). The pollen tube grows through the style to the ovule, entering the micropyle (porogamy). It discharges two male gametes into the embryo sac.

  1. Syngamy: one male gamete fuses with the egg to form the diploid zygote (2n).
  2. Triple fusion: the other male gamete fuses with the two polar nuclei to form the primary endosperm nucleus (3n), which is the specific feature of angiosperms.

After fertilisation.

  1. The zygote forms the embryo (plumule, radicle and cotyledons), the PEN forms the endosperm (triploid, food storage), the integuments form the seed coat, the ovule becomes the seed and the ovary becomes the fruit (the pericarp).
  2. Albuminous seeds retain endosperm (wheat, castor) and non-albuminous seeds use it up (pea, bean). In the false fruits (apple) other parts, such as the thalamus, also grow.
  3. Parthenocarpy forms fruit without fertilisation (banana), and apomixis forms seeds without fertilisation (some grasses). Polyembryony is the presence of more than one embryo in a seed (citrus, mango).

Numerical. If 2n = 24 in the plant, the endosperm has 3n = 36 chromosomes and the egg has 12. Each embryo sac needs 2 male gametes, so 500 ovules need 1000 male gametes, and so 500 pollen tubes. A fruit with 20 seeds needs 20 fertilised ovules.

Conclusion. Double fertilisation gives a 2n embryo and a 3n endosperm in one event, and the ovary and ovule change into the fruit and seed.
